name: Rhinoplasty

card.summary: Surgery that reshapes the nose for looks or breathing; the most discussed facial 'harmony' operation in looksmaxxing, with real revision and complication rates.
card.note: Swelling can take a year to settle, and revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of cases according to published figures.

quick.overview:
Rhinoplasty is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose, or improves breathing. It is done for cosmetic reasons, for functional ones such as an obstructed airway, and for reconstruction after injury, birth defects or cancer. Surgery limited to the septum is called septoplasty.

In looksmaxxing communities the nose is treated as a central feature of facial harmony, and rhinoplasty is frequently discussed alongside jaw surgery and fillers. Published sources describe it as a long-established operation, with high reported satisfaction in several studies but also a meaningful revision rate and a need for psychological screening before cosmetic surgery.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons reshape the nasal bones and cartilages, adding, removing or repositioning tissue, and sometimes grafting cartilage from the septum, ear or rib. Access is either through incisions inside the nose (closed) or with an added incision across the columella (open). Preservation techniques try to keep the existing dorsum rather than cutting it down [1][4].
quick.risks: Reported complications include breathing impairment, asymmetry, collapse of tip support and prolonged swelling that can take up to a year to resolve; smoking impairs healing [1]. Secondary (revision) surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of operations, and revisions are technically harder [1]. Body dysmorphic disorder is more common among cosmetic surgery patients and is associated with dissatisfaction, which is why screening is recommended [3][8].

lead: Rhinoplasty, informally a 'nose job', is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose or improves its function. It takes two broad forms: reconstructive surgery, which restores form and function after injury, birth defects or failed earlier surgery, and cosmetic surgery, which changes appearance [1]. Surgery limited to the septum is called septoplasty [1].

The operation has an unusually long history, with nasal repair described in the Edwin Smith Papyrus and in the Sushruta Samhita of ancient India, and a modern endonasal technique reported by John Orlando Roe in 1887 [1]. Common cosmetic goals include reducing a dorsal hump, narrowing the nostrils or tip, and changing the nasolabial angle [1]. Techniques now include open and closed approaches, cartilage grafting, ultrasonic (piezoelectric) bone cutting, and dorsal preservation [1][2].

Within looksmaxxing forums, rhinoplasty is among the most discussed surgeries, often described as a change in 'facial harmony' and compared against jaw surgery and fillers. Published sources report that revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of cases and that swelling can last up to a year [1]. Researchers recommend screening cosmetic surgery candidates for body dysmorphic disorder [8].
infobox: Can persist up to a year [1]

paras: Rhinoplasty can address function, appearance or both. Functional goals include relieving obstruction through septoplasty, turbinate reduction or spreader grafts; cosmetic goals include reducing a hump, refining the tip and changing nasal angles; reconstructive uses include repair after trauma, birth defects, cancer, autoimmune damage, intranasal drug damage and failed primary surgery [1]. Specialised reviews cover non-Caucasian rhinoplasty, feminisation rhinoplasty, dorsal preservation, cleft rhinoplasty and nonsurgical (filler-based) rhinoplasty [2][4][5][6][7].

In open rhinoplasty a columellar incision is added to the usual internal incisions, giving better visibility and tip control and generally being preferred for revision surgery. Closed rhinoplasty keeps all incisions inside the nose and involves less dissection, less swelling and scarring, a shorter operation and faster recovery. Wikipedia reports that systematic reviews found no significant long-term difference in functional or aesthetic outcome scores between the two, and that surgeon expertise and anatomy drive the choice [1].

Grafts of cartilage from the septum, ear or rib, or of bone, are used to support the nose, with synthetic implants used only when autologous tissue is unavailable; septal extension grafts offer more control of tip projection than columellar struts [1]. Ultrasonic (piezoelectric) instruments cut bone while sparing soft tissue, a technique introduced by Massimo Robiony in 2004 [1]. Dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, which keeps the existing nasal dorsum, has been reviewed in the surgical literature [4].

An AI-generated encyclopedia entry reports satisfaction of roughly 89-93% in several studies of rib-cartilage and hybrid techniques, about 75-85% satisfaction after revision surgery, and a 2018 blinded observer study of 473 raters in which rhinoplasty improved perceived attractiveness, success and health; these figures are unsourced in the entry and should be read with caution [8]. Measures such as the nasofrontal angle (about 115-130 degrees) and tip projection ratio are used in profile assessment, according to the same entry [8].

Wikipedia notes that over-aggressive surgery can impair breathing and cause asymmetry, collapse, a pinched tip or a scooped profile, that swelling can take at least a year to resolve, and that smoking impairs healing [1]. A single dose of corticosteroid has limited evidence of reducing swelling and bleeding for the first two days [1]. Secondary rhinoplasty is needed in about 5-20% of operations and is harder because support structures are often damaged in the first operation [1].

The AI-generated entry reports overall complication rates of about 4-18.8%, mostly minor, with infection around 1-2%, septal perforation about 2% and mortality under 0.01%, and says a 2025 meta-analysis of ethnicity-tailored approaches found fewer complications and revisions than conventional methods; these figures should be verified against primary sources [8].

A 2016 systematic review published in Body Image estimated the weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder in different clinical settings, including cosmetic surgery [3]. The AI-generated entry reports that BDD affects up to about 15% of cosmetic surgery patients, that standardised screening is recommended, and that untreated BDD is associated with dissatisfaction and multiple revisions [8]. Wikipedia says surgeons assess a patient's psychological motivation before surgery [1].

Forum members present the nose as central to midface harmony. One long looksmax.org thread argues that wide alar bases, weak projection or ski-slope bridges limit a face, that fillers only camouflage while rhinoplasty permanently reshapes bone and cartilage, and names celebrities it says benefited, and another user pointed out that the examples were all women [9]. Other threads debate rhinoplasty against jaw surgery for a 'pretty boy' look [10], argue that rhinoplasty is 'cope' for men [11], collect rhinoplasty 'morphs' [12], and report disappointing results [13] or question why many Asian rhinoplasty results look unnatural [14]. In one thread an 18-year-old describes being offered a free rhinoplasty when only a septoplasty was medically needed and asks whether to take it, with a reply saying a free operation is still free [15].

Randomised and controlled trials in rhinoplasty have mostly studied perioperative issues rather than aesthetic outcomes. Examples in the published record include a 1994 trial on the nasal hinge [16], a 1989 trial of steroids in rhinoplasty [17], a 1997 trial of clonidine as premedication [18], a 2023 trial on the effects of burr-assisted rhinoplasty on hearing [19], a 2024 trial of peroperative cooling [20] and a 2026 trial on postoperative pain management [21]. Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include a completed 2024 trial of step count and edema after rhinoplasty [22], a completed trial of a columella strut's effect on tip rotation [23] and a completed trial examining preservation rhinoplasty and nasal valve angle and area [24]. Outcome-measurement papers include general studies of patient benefit from ENT surgery and of outcomes in facial plastic and aesthetic surgery [25][26].

timeline.event: The Edwin Smith Papyrus gives the first mention of repairing a broken nose. [1]
Gasparo Tagliacozzi publishes a method using a biceps pedicle flap. [1]
John Orlando Roe performs the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty. [1]
Jacques Joseph describes nose reduction through internal incisions. [1]
Aurel Rethi introduces the open approach. [1]
Maurice Cottle describes septum-preserving techniques that favour the closed approach. [1]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums rhinoplasty is regarded as a high-impact facial surgery, with long threads on technique, morphs, surgeon choice and results [9][10][13].

claims.claim: The nose drives midface harmony, so reshaping it changes the whole face.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster says the nose is 'center stage', that it dictates midface harmony, and that angles such as nasofrontal and nasolabial separate average from striking faces [9].
claims.experts: Surgical references describe profile measurements such as the nasofrontal angle and tip projection ratio [8]. A blinded observer study cited by an AI-generated encyclopedia entry reports raters judged post-rhinoplasty faces as more attractive, successful and healthy, although that figure is unsourced [8].

claims.claim: Fillers only camouflage, while surgery permanently reshapes bone and cartilage.
claims.believers: The same poster says fillers can only camouflage the nose while rhinoplasty reshapes the underlying structure [9].
claims.experts: Reviews of nonsurgical rhinoplasty exist in the surgical literature [6][7]. Wikipedia says surgery carries a 5-20% revision rate and swelling that may last a year [1].

claims.claim: Rhinoplasty can go wrong and make a face look worse or 'fake'.
claims.believers: Thread titles on looksmax.org report that rhinoplasty 'made me uglier' [13] and ask why many Asian rhinoplasty results look 'fake' [14].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that over-aggressive surgery can cause asymmetry, collapse or a pinched tip, and that revisions are needed in roughly 5-20% of cases [1].

claims.believers: A thread titled 'rhinoplasty is cope for men' disputes whether nose surgery is worthwhile for male faces [11]; the debate is also framed against jaw surgery [10].
claims.experts: No published study in the sources reviewed compares male nose surgery with jaw surgery for attractiveness; the AI-generated entry notes women make up about 80% of patients [8].
